Recurrent vaginitis ≥3 episodes/year → extended induction then weekly fluconazole for 6 months
Candidemia → IV micafungin and blood cultures; investigate/remove infected catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Poor oral intake, painful fissures, recurrent vaginitis; invasive disease → endophthalmitis, endocarditis, organ abscesses
Azoles: hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, CYP interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rinse mouth after inhaled steroids; clean dentures, keep folds dry, change wet diapers promptly
Optimize glucose control and HIV ART; routine partner treatment unnecessary for uncomplicated vaginitis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Leukoplakia/oral hairy leukoplakia: white plaques do not scrape off
Irritant diaper dermatitis: spares folds; bacterial vaginosis: fishy odor, elevated vaginal pH

table.title: Superficial presentations
rows: Beefy erythema, satellite pustules; folds involved
Topical azole or single-dose oral fluconazole

cervicitis-pid.name: Cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
cervicitis-pid.core: Sexually active patient with mucopurulent discharge or postcoital bleeding; ascending infection adds pelvic pain, sometimes an adnexal abscess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25 (adolescent cervical ectopy → vulnerable columnar epithelium), new/multiple partners, inconsistent condoms, prior STI
IUD-associated PID risk concentrated within first 3 weeks after insertion

rows.label: Clues
items: Cervical friability, easily induced endocervical bleeding; infection sometimes asymptomatic
Dyspareunia, fever; severe unilateral pain/adnexal mass → **tubo-ovarian abscess**
Peritonitis, shock → rupture; RUQ pain → Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis
Persistent dysuria, sterile pyuria, negative culture → chlamydial urethritis, not UTI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GC/CT ascend cervix → endometrium/tubes; PID often polymicrobial, including anaerobes
Chlamydial tubal damage: **host immune response** → scarring, hydrosalpinx

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test** first; vaginal/cervical or urine **GC/CT NAAT**; HIV/syphilis testing
★ Pelvic pain + **cervical motion, uterine, OR adnexal tenderness** → presumptive PID; no confirmation delay
Negative cervical NAAT does not exclude upper-tract infection; normal discharge/no vaginal leukocytes argues against PID
**Transvaginal US** for abscess or diagnostic uncertainty; routine laparoscopy unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cervicitis: empiric GC/CT coverage IF high risk/unreliable follow-up; otherwise await NAAT
★ Admit IF **pregnant, abscess, severe illness**, oral intolerance, uncertain surgical diagnosis, or failure by 72 h
Abscess rupture → emergency surgery; persistent abscess after 48–72 h antibiotics → drainage
Pregnant chlamydia → **azithromycin**, avoid doxycycline; retain IUD initially, reassess if no improvement

rows.label: Complications
items: Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; abscess → sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from prior **60 days**; abstain until courses completed, partners treated, symptoms resolved
Retest GC/CT at 3 months; pregnant chlamydia → test of cure at 4 weeks
Annual GC/CT screening: sexually active women <25, older women with risks; condoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt unilateral pain, vomiting; Doppler flow may persist
Appendicitis: migrating RLQ pain, CT appendiceal inflammation

table.title: Antibiotic branches
rows: Ceftriaxone; add CT regimen unless excluded
Oral drugs 14 days; ceftriaxone once IM outpatient

child-growth-and-development.name: Child growth and development
child-growth-and-development.scope: Normal growth velocity, weight doubling and tripling milestones, WHO/CDC growth chart interpretation, developmental surveillance, normal toddler behavioral variants (head banging, temper tantrums)
child-growth-and-development.core: Interpret serial growth and developmental progress against age, family pattern, and corrected gestational age; a trajectory matters more than one percentile.

rows.label: Definition
items: Weight doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 12 months, quadruples near 24 months
Length increases about 25 cm during year 1; prepubertal height velocity about 5–6 cm/year
★ **WHO charts before 2 years; CDC charts from 2 years** in US practice

rows.label: Interpret
items: Nutrition failure: weight falls first; endocrine disease: height slows with preserved/increased weight
★ Falling **2 major percentile channels**, well child → **diet diary, calorie counts** before labs
Correct prematurity through about 2 years; track infant head circumference

rows.label: Use when
items: Developmental surveillance every visit; standardized general screens at 9, 18, and 30 months
★ **Regression/missed milestones → early intervention**; language delay → **audiometry** before speech testing
BMI-for-age from 2 years; weight-for-length younger; consider parental heights and pubertal timing

rows.label: Compare
items: Tantrums, picky eating, bedtime separation distress → reassure, routines, calm limits; no sedatives
Head banging at sleep onset or frustration, normal development → self-soothing; assess injuries
Preschool restlessness, good function → no stimulants; overwhelmed parent → **parenting classes**

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **One percentile cannot diagnose disease**; stable tracking + normal exam → reassure
Persistent skill loss needs evaluation; never wait for school failure
Short parents, normal bone age → familial; average parents, delayed puberty → **constitutional delay**

rows.label: Adolescence
items: ★ Moodiness, privacy, family detachment, rule-questioning, late bedtimes, good function → reassure, educate parents
Parental-pressure conflict, occasional experimentation, no impairment → not ODD, substance use disorder
Weight worry, stable percentile, normal BMI, regular menses → normal; not eating disorder

table.title: Normal by age
rows: Holds head up; not yet reaching
Sits unsupported; bangs blocks, self-feeds finger foods
Walks; scribbles; non-walker at 14 months normal
Balances on one foot; copies circle
Same-sex parent preference; involve other parent otherwise

child-growth-and-development.evidence: Checked screening ages 2026-10-30: [AAP surveillance/screening](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/); growth facts established pediatric teaching.

colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.name: Colorectal polyps and polyposis syndromes
colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.scope: Adenomatous polyps, serrated polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis
colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.core: Colorectal polyps differ in malignant potential; numerous lesions or characteristic extraintestinal findings suggest an inherited cancer syndrome.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, smoking; pathogenic germline variants in hereditary polyposis

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually incidental; occult bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia; large distal polyps may prolapse
Childhood painless rectal bleeding → solitary juvenile polyp; recurrent pain → hamartoma-associated intussusception
★ **Mucocutaneous lip pigmentation** with hamartomatous polyps → Peutz-Jeghers
Serrated crypts: proximal sessile lesions premalignant, unlike typical small distal hyperplastic polyps

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conventional adenomas progress through dysplasia; sessile serrated lesions follow a distinct molecular pathway
Hamartomas contain disorganized native tissue; syndromic forms carry cancer risk despite benign-appearing histology

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with complete polypectomy and histology** defines type and surveillance
Advanced adenoma: ≥10 mm, villous component, or high-grade dysplasia
Numerous adenomas, young age, syndromic features → genetic counseling/testing
≥5 juvenile colorectal polyps, other GI juvenile polyps, or family history → juvenile polyposis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove adenomatous/serrated lesions; incomplete or unresectable lesion → advanced endoscopy or surgery
FAP → **prophylactic colectomy** when burden/dysplasia cannot be controlled; continue retained-rectum surveillance
Hamartomatous syndromes → endoscopic removal of large/symptomatic polyps; surgery for obstruction or uncontrolled burden

rows.label: Complications
items: Colorectal cancer; postpolypectomy bleeding/perforation; intussusception and anemia in hamartomatous disease
FAP → duodenal cancer, desmoid tumors; Peutz-Jeghers → pancreatic, breast and gynecologic cancers

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Family cascade testing; syndrome-specific colon and upper-GI surveillance
Low-risk 1–2 small tubular adenomas → repeat colonoscopy 7–10 years after high-quality examination
Advanced adenoma → generally 3 years; shorten for large piecemeal resection or numerous lesions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sporadic hyperplastic polyp: small rectosigmoid lesion, usually negligible cancer risk
Lynch syndrome: few polyps, mismatch-repair defect, colorectal/endometrial cancers

colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.evidence: Surveillance checked 2026-10-30: [US Multi-Society Task Force, 2020](https://www.asge.org/home/resources/publications/guidelines/recommendations-for-follow-up-after-colonoscopy-and-polypectomy-a-consensus-update-by-the-us-multi-society-task-force-on-colorectal-cancer); syndromes: established teaching.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.core: Newborn salt loss or atypical genitalia demands adrenal evaluation; hypertension with abnormal puberty suggests a different steroid-synthesis block.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive inheritance; affected sibling, consanguinity
Classic disease presents neonatally; partial enzyme deficiency may present with adolescent androgen excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Neonatal vomiting, weight loss, dehydration, **shock**, ↓Na, ↓glucose → salt-wasting adrenal crisis
46,XX virilization with internal female organs; 46,XY infants may lack obvious external warning signs
Nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency: premature pubarche, hirsutism, acne or irregular menses

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Low cortisol removes feedback → ↑ACTH and adrenal hyperplasia
Steroid precursors accumulate upstream; androgen and mineralocorticoid effects depend on enzyme block

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **17-hydroxyprogesterone** screens for 21-hydroxylase deficiency; elevated values → confirmatory steroid testing
Borderline nonclassic disease → ACTH-stimulated 17-OHP; electrolytes, renin, cortisol and androgens guide subtype
Ambiguous genitalia → karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, endocrine consultation; avoid premature sex assignment
Newborn screen may miss milder disease; clinical instability overrides screening results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crisis → **IV hydrocortisone**, isotonic saline, dextrose; treat severe hyperkalemia
Glucocorticoid replacement suppresses ACTH; salt-wasting forms → fludrocortisone plus infant salt supplementation
11β/17α-associated hypertension → glucocorticoids; add antihypertensives for persistent elevation
Genital differences → multidisciplinary counseling; timing of surgery requires informed shared decisions

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated crisis → death; androgen excess → precocious pseudopuberty, advanced bone age, short adult height
Excess replacement → growth suppression, obesity, osteoporosis; inadequate replacement → infertility/adrenal rest tumors

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Newborn screening, genetic counseling; emergency steroid kit, medical alert, illness/surgery stress dosing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Androgen insensitivity: 46,XY, testes, absent uterus, normal adrenal steroids
Pyloric stenosis: vomiting with hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis rather than salt-wasting hyperkalemia

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

foodborne-illnesses.name: Foodborne illnesses
foodborne-illnesses.scope: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens, scombroid, ciguatera, Salmonella, Campylobacter
foodborne-illnesses.core: Incubation time and the dominant symptom separate preformed-toxin vomiting from intestinal infection requiring selective stool testing and antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Food improperly refrigerated/reheated; shared-meal outbreaks; raw poultry/eggs, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat
Infancy, older age, immunosuppression or vascular disease increase invasive Salmonella risk
Improperly chilled tuna/mackerel → scombroid; tropical reef fish → ciguatera

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt short-lived emesis without fever favors ingested toxin; inflammatory enteritis → fever or bloody stools
★ **Severe dehydration, bacteremia signs or persistent bloody diarrhea** → urgent assessment
Campylobacter pain may mimic appendicitis; poultry exposure supports both major invasive enteric pathogens
Fish toxins: scombroid → flushing/urticaria; ciguatera → paresthesias, hot/cold temperature reversal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ingested enterotoxins act rapidly; scombroid: histamine; ciguatoxin activates voltage-gated sodium channels
Invasive mucosal infection induces inflammation and can permit bloodstream spread
S aureus: **heat-stable** preformed enterotoxin builds in unrefrigerated food; cooking does not destroy it

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild brief outbreak illness → **clinical diagnosis**, usually no stool studies
Fever, bloody/mucoid stool, severe tenderness or sepsis → stool PCR/culture including Shiga toxin testing
Suspected bacteremia → blood cultures; report suspected outbreaks to public health

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scombroid → **diphenhydramine/famotidine**; anaphylaxis → epinephrine; ciguatera → supportive care
Oral rehydration; severe dehydration → IV isotonic fluids; toxin syndromes do not benefit from antibiotics
Campylobacter severe/prolonged or high-risk illness → azithromycin; most mild cases resolve untreated
Nontyphoidal Salmonella: severe/invasive or high-risk host → ceftriaxone or susceptibility-directed antibiotic
★ Suspected **STEC → avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs**; hemolytic uremic syndrome risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Campylobacter → Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis; Salmonella → bacteremia, vascular infection, sickle-cell osteomyelitis
Volume depletion → AKI; antibiotics may prolong uncomplicated Salmonella carriage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Cook poultry/eggs thoroughly; separate raw foods, rapid refrigeration, handwashing; avoid unpasteurized products

rows.label: Mimics
items: Norovirus: contagious outbreak with vomiting and diarrhea
Appendicitis: focal progressive peritoneal findings; toxin illness usually self-limited

foodborne-illnesses.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC marine toxins](https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/food-poisoning-from-marine-toxins.html), CDC Salmonella/Campylobacter and IDSA infectious-diarrhea guidance.

table.title: Timing after exposure
rows: Vomiting; cream pastries, mayonnaise salads, handled meats

foreign-body-aspiration.name: Foreign body aspiration
foreign-body-aspiration.scope: Pediatric airway foreign body, choking maneuvers, rigid bronchoscopy, chest x-ray findings (air trapping, atelectasis), observation of partial obstruction
foreign-body-aspiration.core: Abrupt choking with unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests airway foreign body, even with normal radiographs.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Children <3 years exploring objects orally; nuts, seeds, grapes, hot dogs, toy fragments
Neurologic swallowing impairment, sedation, intoxication, poor dentition in adults

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed coughing/gagging during eating or play; symptoms may partially resolve after initial event
★ **Cannot speak, cough effectively, or breathe** → severe airway obstruction
Proximal obstruction: stridor; distal obstruction: focal wheeze, persistent cough, recurrent same-lobe pneumonia
Cyanosis, altered consciousness, exhaustion → imminent respiratory arrest

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Partial ball-valve blockage allows inspiration but limits expiration → distal hyperinflation
Complete bronchial blockage → resorption atelectasis; retained organic material causes inflammation and infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable child → **chest x-ray**, including expiratory or bilateral decubitus views when feasible
Unilateral air trapping, mediastinal shift, collapse, or radiopaque object may identify location
Most food objects are radiolucent; negative examination/imaging does not exclude a convincing history
★ High suspicion → **bronchoscopy**; avoid delaying definitive evaluation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: Effective cough/partial obstruction → encourage coughing, observe closely; no blind finger sweep
★ Infant severe choking: **5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts**, repeat
Age ≥1 year: cycles of five back blows/five abdominal thrusts; pregnancy/marked obesity → chest thrusts
Unresponsive → CPR, inspect mouth during airway opening, remove visible object only
★ Stable retained pediatric object → **rigid bronchoscopy** for retrieval; expert airway team for unstable obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrest, postobstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis, granulation tissue
Removal can cause bleeding, edema, or pneumothorax; persistent symptoms need reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid small hard foods/toys; cut grapes lengthwise, supervise eating, avoid running with food
Teach caregivers choking response; keep small objects away from young children

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent diffuse wheeze with bronchodilator response
Croup: preceding URI, barking cough, diffuse upper-airway obstruction
Bronchiolitis: viral prodrome, diffuse crackles/wheezing in an infant

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder
Hysterectomy/pelvic surgery → ureteral ligation: flank pain, fever, unilateral hydroureteronephrosis; not pyelonephritis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention, perineal/scrotal hematoma or high-riding prostate → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Blunt flank trauma → **urinalysis**; stable, no hematuria → **no further testing** unless high-energy deceleration
Stable gross hematuria, or microscopic + hypotension → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images, not laparotomy
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; absent flow or high clinical suspicion → immediate exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

gestational-diabetes-mellitus.name: Gestational diabetes mellitus
gestational-diabetes-mellitus.scope: Screening (50g oral glucose challenge at 24-28 weeks), diagnostic 3-hour 100g test, glycemic targets, nutritional therapy, insulin, fetal and neonatal complications (macrosomia, hypoglycemia, RDS, polycythemia)
gestational-diabetes-mellitus.core: Pregnancy-induced insulin resistance unmasks hyperglycemia, increasing fetal insulin secretion and growth; screen routinely at 24–28 weeks.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, prior GDM/macrosomia, family history of type 2 diabetes, PCOS
High-risk patients need early assessment for previously unrecognized overt diabetes

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; excessive fetal growth or polyhydramnios may prompt evaluation
Early marked hyperglycemia suggests preexisting diabetes rather than typical later-onset GDM

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental hormones increase maternal insulin requirements; inadequate beta-cell compensation causes dysglycemia
Maternal glucose crosses placenta; insulin does not; fetal hyperinsulinemia persists briefly after birth
Fetal hyperinsulinemia → macrosomia; antagonizes cortisol → less surfactant, **RDS**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Two-step screen: **nonfasting 50 g challenge**, 1-hour threshold 130–140 mg/dL by local protocol
Positive challenge → fasting 100 g, 3-hour OGTT; **≥2 abnormal values** diagnose GDM
Alternative one-step 75 g OGTT: fasting ≥92, 1-hour ≥180, or 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL
HbA1c alone does not replace pregnancy glucose testing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First: **individualized nutrition, activity, home glucose monitoring**; avoid severe carbohydrate restriction
★ Targets: fasting **<95**, 1-hour <140, or 2-hour <120 mg/dL
Above targets despite lifestyle → **insulin preferred**; metformin crosses placenta, counsel if used
Medication need or poor control → fetal surveillance; delivery timing depends on control and obstetric findings
Suspected fetal weight ≥4,500 g with diabetes → discuss planned cesarean

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal: preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, future type 2 diabetes
Fetal: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma; poor control increases stillbirth risk
Neonate: **hypoglycemia**, RDS, polycythemia, jaundice; congenital anomalies mainly reflect pregestational diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Postpartum **75 g OGTT at 4–12 weeks**; lifelong diabetes testing every 1–3 years
Breastfeeding, weight management, activity; most GDM insulin needs resolve after placental delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pregestational diabetes: overt diagnostic-range hyperglycemia early in pregnancy
Physiologic glycosuria: lower renal threshold without diagnostic blood glucose abnormalities

glomerulonephritis.name: Glomerulonephritis
glomerulonephritis.scope: Nephritic syndrome, poststreptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GN (anti-GBM, ANCA), lupus nephritis, RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria quantification, kidney biopsy
glomerulonephritis.core: Glomerular inflammation causes hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema, and reduced filtration; rapidly rising creatinine demands urgent evaluation for crescentic disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent streptococcal pharyngitis/skin infection, systemic autoimmunity, small-vessel vasculitis
IgA nephropathy often follows mucosal infection; anti-GBM pulmonary bleeding risk increases with smoking

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs** identify a glomerular bleeding source
Tea-colored urine, oliguria, periorbital swelling; nephrotic-range protein loss can coexist
★ **Hemoptysis + AKI** → pulmonary–renal syndrome; rapidly progressive disease may initially lack systemic symptoms

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune complexes, basement-membrane antibodies, or pauci-immune vascular injury inflame glomerular capillaries
Crescent formation compresses capillary tufts → rapid, potentially irreversible loss of filtration
Reduced filtration → sodium/water retention → **volume overload**, edema, hypertension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urinalysis/microscopy → **creatinine, electrolytes, urine protein/creatinine ratio**; monitor urine output
C3/C4, ANA/dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM; ASO/anti-DNase B when poststreptococcal disease suspected
★ **Kidney biopsy** for rapidly progressive AKI, substantial persistent proteinuria, or uncertain systemic GN
Typical childhood poststreptococcal course may not require biopsy; persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks warrants reassessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Salt restriction, loop diuretics for overload, BP control; ACE inhibitor/ARB for persistent proteinuria when stable
★ Pulmonary–renal/RPGN → **urgent nephrology, steroids + immunosuppression** before irreversible decline
Anti-GBM: plasma exchange + cyclophosphamide; ANCA: rituximab/cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange only selected severe cases
Lupus: biopsy-directed mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide + steroids; poststreptococcal disease mainly supportive

rows.label: Complications
items: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, CKD; dialysis for refractory life-threatening derangements
Immunosuppression → infection, cytopenias, infertility with cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP/proteinuria, avoid nephrotoxins, follow renal function and urine findings

rows.label: Mimics
items: ATN: muddy-brown casts after ischemia/toxins
Urologic bleeding: isomorphic RBCs, clots, no RBC casts

glomerulonephritis.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching.

hemolytic-anemias.name: Hemolytic Anemias
hemolytic-anemias.scope: autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold agglutinins), hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, DAT/Coombs testing, peripheral smear, complications
hemolytic-anemias.core: Reticulocytosis, elevated LDH/indirect bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin suggest hemolysis; DAT and smear identify the mechanism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune disease, CLL, drugs → immune hemolysis; infections can trigger cold-antibody disease
Family history → inherited membrane/enzyme defect; oxidants, fava beans or infection trigger G6PD crises
Coombs-negative newborn jaundice after maternal oxidant drug → consider G6PD; X-linked, Mediterranean ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine; splenomegaly suggests chronic extravascular destruction
Severe intravascular lysis → hemoglobinuria, back pain, AKI; hemoglobin decline can outpace reticulocyte response
Spherocytes occur in hereditary and warm immune disease; morphology alone cannot distinguish them
Childhood gallstones + splenomegaly + family history → hereditary spherocytosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extravascular: splenic/hepatic macrophage clearance; intravascular: RBC destruction within circulation
Free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin; marrow compensates unless infection, deficiency or marrow failure limits production
Hereditary spherocytosis: ankyrin/spectrin cytoskeleton defect changes RBC shape → trapping in splenic red pulp

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin**, peripheral smear
★ **DAT/Coombs** detects immune coating; negative test redirects toward nonimmune causes
Hereditary spherocytosis → eosin-5-maleimide binding test; usually normocytic, normochromic; ↑MCHC supports
G6PD activity can be falsely normal during crisis/after transfusion → repeat after recovery
Schistocytes → evaluate microangiopathy/mechanical destruction urgently, including platelet count and renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe symptomatic anemia → **transfuse promptly** with blood-bank coordination; do not await perfect compatibility
Warm AIHA → glucocorticoids; refractory → rituximab or selected splenectomy
Cold disease → warmth, treat cause; rituximab-based treatment when symptomatic; steroids usually ineffective
G6PD → stop oxidant, treat trigger, supportive transfusion when severe
Hereditary spherocytosis → folate; selected severe disease → splenectomy after immunization

rows.label: Complications
items: Pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis; chronic immune disease increases thrombosis risk
Splenectomy → encapsulated infection and thrombosis; intravascular disease → renal injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ G6PD: avoid **dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, sulfonamides** and other oxidants
Before splenectomy: pneumococcal/meningococcal/Hib vaccines; infection education and selected antibiotic prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blood loss: reticulocytosis without hemolytic chemistry
Gilbert syndrome: isolated indirect bilirubin without anemia

table.title: Mechanism signatures
rows: Bite cells; Heinz bodies on supravital stain

hemolytic-anemias.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology teaching.

hypoglycemia.name: Hypoglycemia
hypoglycemia.scope: Drug-induced hypoglycemia (insulin, sulfonylureas), Whipple triad, acute management (dextrose, glucagon), insulinoma
hypoglycemia.core: Compatible symptoms, documented low plasma glucose, and relief with correction establish Whipple triad and justify evaluation for a hypoglycemic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Insulin, sulfonylureas; missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney failure increase risk
Sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency; insulinoma causes fasting episodes in otherwise well adults
Child, illness, poor intake or sugar-free fluids → **glycogen depletion**, ketotic hypoglycemia ± anion-gap acidosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Adrenergic: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger; neuroglycopenic: confusion, visual change, seizures, coma
Autonomic neuropathy or recurrent episodes may blunt warning symptoms
★ Glucose **<54 mg/dL** clinically significant; diabetes alert threshold <70 mg/dL

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Excess insulin suppresses glucose output and ketones; substrate/hormone deficits impair counterregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; plasma confirmation if discordant, never delay emergency correction
Critical sample: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, sulfonylurea screen
Suspected endogenous fasting disorder → supervised fast up to 72 h; mixed-meal test for postprandial symptoms
Biochemically confirmed insulinoma → pancreatic CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound if localization unclear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Awake and swallowing → **15 g rapid carbohydrate**, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if needed
★ Altered or unable to swallow → **IV dextrose**; no IV access → IM/intranasal glucagon
After recovery → longer-acting carbohydrate; glucagon less effective after alcohol or glycogen depletion
★ Sulfonylurea recurrence → **octreotide + dextrose**, prolonged observation; long-acting insulin may require infusion
Adjust diabetes regimen and treat trigger; localized insulinoma → surgical resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Seizures, brain injury, arrhythmias, falls; recurrent episodes cause impaired awareness
Dextrose alone after sulfonylurea exposure may stimulate further insulin release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Meal/exercise planning, glucose monitoring or CGM alarms, caregiver rescue-glucagon education
Relax overly intensive targets when recurrent events, frailty, or impaired awareness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic attack: normal glucose during symptoms
Stroke: focal deficit may persist after glucose correction; evaluate both if unresolved

hypoglycemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine diagnostic and hypoglycemia treatment principles.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, family history of autoimmune disease; thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass
Congenital primary → **thyroid dysgenesis** most common, not lymphocytic thyroiditis

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease
Infant: macroglossia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, large fontanelle → **TSH/free T4**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic infiltration; firm painless goiter, even if euthyroid; **anti-TPO/antithyroglobulin** antibodies

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Fasting, apart from calcium/iron; TSH at 6–8 weeks; **persistently high → increase dose**, even if asymptomatic
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical, untreated: generally start at TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression, dementia, psychosis: normal TSH; hypothyroidism itself can cause reversible cognitive or psychiatric symptoms
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation and reflexes generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
Proximal weakness + ↑CK → EMG/nerve conduction (myopathic pattern); MRI guides **muscle biopsy**
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs
Guillain-Barré: ascending distal-predominant weakness, areflexia

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

inherited-bleeding-disorders.name: Inherited bleeding disorders
inherited-bleeding-disorders.scope: Hemophilia A, Hemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, factor XI deficiency, hemarthrosis, mixing studies, factor VIII inhibitors
inherited-bleeding-disorders.core: Deep tissue bleeding suggests a coagulation-factor defect; mucosal bleeding suggests platelet/von Willebrand dysfunction, even with a normal platelet count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemophilia A/B: X-linked, usually males; maternal family history may be absent
vWD usually autosomal dominant; factor XI deficiency autosomal, enriched in Ashkenazi ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Recurrent **hemarthroses**, muscle hematomas and delayed postoperative bleeding → hemophilia
Epistaxis, gingival bleeding, easy bruising and heavy menses → vWD
Factor XI deficiency: variable postsurgical bleeding, especially oral/urologic procedures; hemarthrosis uncommon
Unexpected major bleeding after circumcision or surgery may reveal previously undiagnosed disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: VIII/IX/XI deficits impair intrinsic-pathway thrombin generation and fibrin stabilization
vWF mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII; deficiency impairs primary and sometimes secondary hemostasis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC/platelets, PT, aPTT; **mixing study corrects** factor deficiency, fails with inhibitor
Factor VIII, IX or XI activity identifies deficiency; hemophilia generally normal PT/platelets
★ Suspected vWD → **vWF antigen, activity and factor VIII**; aPTT may be normal
Stress, pregnancy and estrogen raise vWF; repeat borderline testing when clinically stable
Severe hemophilia: factor activity <1%; inhibitor testing if replacement response is inadequate

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Major suspected hemophilic bleeding → **replace deficient factor immediately**, before imaging delays
Hemophilia A → factor VIII; B → factor IX; emicizumab prophylaxis for selected A
Mild responsive A or type 1 vWD → **desmopressin after response testing**
Severe vWD → vWF-containing concentrate; avoid desmopressin in type 2B and ineffective type 3
Mucosal bleeding → tranexamic acid; factor XI procedures → antifibrinolytic ± plasma with hematology planning

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic hemarthropathy, intracranial hemorrhage, anemia; factor inhibitors complicate replacement
Desmopressin → water retention/hyponatremia; factor concentrates can increase thrombosis risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Individualized factor/nonfactor prophylaxis, dental care, procedure planning; avoid aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs
Family genetic counseling; fluid restriction and sodium monitoring around desmopressin

rows.label: Mimics
items: ITP: low platelets with mucocutaneous bleeding
Acquired factor VIII inhibitor: new bleeding, mixing fails to correct
Vitamin K deficiency: PT prolonged first

lyme-disease.name: Lyme disease
lyme-disease.scope: Borrelia burgdorferi, erythema migrans, early localized, early disseminated, late Lyme arthritis, doxycycline, ceftriaxone
lyme-disease.core: Ixodes-transmitted Borrelia infection progresses from an expanding skin lesion to neurologic, cardiac, or joint disease when untreated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Wooded/brush exposure in Northeast, mid-Atlantic, upper Midwest; attached blacklegged tick
Tick exposure may be unnoticed; small-mammal reservoirs sustain transmission

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Erythema migrans**: enlarging lesion >5 cm, days after bite; central clearing not required
Early dissemination: multiple lesions, unilateral/**bilateral facial palsy**, lymphocytic meningitis, fluctuating AV block
Late disease: intermittent large-joint swelling, especially knee; severe pain less prominent than effusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete inoculation → local multiplication, hematogenous spread, inflammatory injury
Persistent antibodies can remain after cure and do not prove viable infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical erythema migrans → **clinical diagnosis**, no serology needed
Other compatible disease → two-tier serology: EIA followed by immunoblot or second EIA
Early localized serology may be negative; isolated IgM after >30 days is unreliable
Joint-fluid PCR supports selected arthritis cases; CSF testing for CNS disease; ECG for cardiac symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized skin disease → **doxycycline 10 days**, or amoxicillin/cefuroxime 14 days
Facial palsy/mild neurologic disease may use oral doxycycline; severe CNS disease → IV ceftriaxone
★ Symptomatic carditis, PR ≥300 ms, higher-degree block → **hospitalize, telemetry, IV ceftriaxone**; pacing if needed
Lyme arthritis → 28-day oral course; persistent objective disease requires reassessment, sometimes IV ceftriaxone
Post-treatment nonspecific fatigue → supportive evaluation; no prolonged antibiotics without objective reinfection/failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Complete heart block, meningoencephalitis, recurrent arthritis, postinfectious joint inflammation
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction shortly after antibiotics; not necessarily drug allergy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ High-risk Ixodes bite, attachment ≥36 hours, endemic region → **single-dose doxycycline within 72 hours of removal**
Tick checks, permethrin-treated clothing, DEET; remove tick with fine tweezers near skin
No prophylaxis for low-risk bite or routine serologic testing of asymptomatic patients

rows.label: Mimics
items: Immediate bite hypersensitivity: small, itchy, does not progressively enlarge
Septic arthritis: marked pain, toxicity, positive culture; babesiosis: hemolysis and intraerythrocytic parasites
Neurosyphilis: Lyme can falsely react on syphilis serology; tick exposure + facial palsy → Borrelia antibodies

muscular-dystrophies.name: Muscular dystrophies
muscular-dystrophies.scope: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin frameshift, Gowers sign, dilated cardiomyopathy), Becker muscular dystrophy, myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeat, myotonia, cataracts, balding), genetic testing
muscular-dystrophies.core: Progressive inherited muscle weakness: childhood pelvic-girdle weakness suggests dystrophinopathy; delayed relaxation with multisystem disease suggests myotonic dystrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Duchenne/Becker: X-linked recessive; affected boys, maternal carrier relatives; de novo variants common
Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant with anticipation; severe congenital disease often maternally transmitted

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Gowers maneuver** and calf pseudohypertrophy indicate proximal weakness
Dystrophinopathy: waddling gait, delayed motor milestones; preserved sensation
Grip/percussion myotonia: delayed muscle relaxation, often improving with repeated movement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dystrophin deficiency destabilizes muscle membrane → myofiber necrosis and fat/fibrous replacement
Myotonic dystrophy: toxic expanded-repeat RNA disrupts splicing in multiple tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK → genetic testing**; dystrophin deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing if needed
Myotonic phenotype → DMPK repeat-expansion testing; muscle biopsy rarely needed
ECG/echocardiography and pulmonary function at diagnosis and serially; assess swallowing and sleep ventilation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Duchenne: **prednisone or deflazacort**, stretching, mobility support; specialist genotype-directed options
Cardiomyopathy → ACE inhibitor/ARB, add beta-blocker; respiratory weakness → assisted cough/noninvasive ventilation
Disabling myotonia → mexiletine after cardiac evaluation; high-grade conduction block → pacemaker
Avoid succinylcholine; dystrophinopathy also carries rhabdomyolysis risk with volatile anesthetics

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, restrictive respiratory failure, aspiration, scoliosis, contractures
Steroid-associated osteoporosis and adrenal suppression; myotonic dystrophy → sudden cardiac death

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Carrier testing and genetic counseling**; screen female dystrophin carriers for cardiomyopathy
Vaccination, nutritional support, bone health monitoring, regular cardiac/respiratory surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: SMA: areflexia, fasciculations, relatively modest CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: acquired weakness, inflammation; no characteristic inheritance pattern

table.title: Distinguishing types
rows: Distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy

muscular-dystrophies.evidence: Not checked online; established phenotypes and supportive treatment; novel genotype-specific treatments omitted.

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery
Volvulus: sudden bilious emesis after normal feeding and meconium; atresia: vomiting from first feeds

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal DJ junction; enema: misplaced cecum
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal surgical teaching.

neonatal-respiratory-distress.name: Neonatal respiratory distress
neonatal-respiratory-distress.scope: Transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration syndrome, persistent PH
neonatal-respiratory-distress.core: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting, or cyanosis after birth requires stabilization while gestational age, delivery history, and imaging narrow the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prematurity/maternal diabetes → RDS; cesarean without labor → TTN; post-term/meconium → aspiration
Maternal fever, prolonged membrane rupture or inadequate GBS prophylaxis raise concern for infectious pneumonia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Apnea, bradycardia, poor perfusion or severe hypoxemia** → immediate neonatal resuscitation
PPHN: labile hypoxemia, preductal right-hand saturation higher than postductal foot saturation
Unilateral absent breath sounds or abrupt deterioration → pneumothorax; scaphoid abdomen → diaphragmatic hernia
TTN improves within 24–72 hours; persistent/worsening disease warrants reassessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Poor lung expansion, airway obstruction or V/Q mismatch impairs oxygenation
PPHN: persistently high pulmonary resistance causes right-to-left ductal/atrial shunting

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry, blood gas and chest radiograph** after initial stabilization
Pre/postductal saturation comparison and echocardiography for suspected PPHN; exclude structural heart disease
Possible infection → blood culture and CBC; biomarkers cannot independently exclude sepsis
Persistent unexplained hypoxemia → echocardiography rather than assuming primary pulmonary disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warmth, oxygen titrated to neonatal targets; **CPAP** for breathing infant with distress
Apnea/gasping or HR <100 → positive-pressure ventilation; ineffective ventilation requires corrective steps/advanced airway
RDS with increasing oxygen need → intratracheal surfactant; mechanical ventilation if noninvasive support fails
★ PPHN → lung recruitment/oxygenation, **inhaled nitric oxide** for suitable term/near-term infants; refractory → ECMO
Meconium: no routine tracheal suction; suction only obstructed ventilation; suspected sepsis → ampicillin/gentamicin

rows.label: Complications
items: Air leak, hypoxic brain injury, death; prematurity/ventilation → bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Antenatal corticosteroids when preterm delivery expected; avoid elective delivery before 39 weeks
Treat maternal infection, provide indicated intrapartum GBS prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cyanotic congenital heart disease: abnormal cardiac anatomy on echo
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: bowel in chest; intubate and decompress stomach, avoid bag-mask ventilation

table.title: Lung patterns
rows: Low volumes, diffuse ground glass/air bronchograms
May be normal or reflect trigger

nephrotic-syndrome.name: Nephrotic syndrome
nephrotic-syndrome.scope: Minimal change, FSGS, membranous, diabetic nephropathy; thrombosis and hyperlipidemia
nephrotic-syndrome.core: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and edema indicates nephrotic syndrome; assess the cause and complications before choosing immunosuppression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, obesity, HIV, hepatitis B/C, autoimmune disease, malignancy and selected medications
Children favor minimal change; obesity, HIV, heroin or reduced nephron mass can cause secondary FSGS

rows.label: Clues
items: Periorbital/dependent edema, foamy urine, weight gain; severe cases → anasarca or effusions
Hyperlipidemia, lipiduria, oval fat bodies/fatty casts; urine sediment often otherwise bland
★ Sudden flank pain, hematuria or falling filtration → **renal vein thrombosis**
Low effective volume may coexist with overload; edema gone + orthostasis/oliguria on diuretic → **overdiuresis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Podocyte barrier damage leaks albumin; sodium retention and low oncotic pressure promote edema
Urinary loss of anticoagulants and immunoglobulins increases thrombosis and infection risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adult protein **>3.5 g/day** or equivalent spot protein/creatinine ratio; serum albumin and lipid profile
Urinalysis/microscopy, renal function, HbA1c; targeted HIV, HBV/HCV, ANA/complement and monoclonal-protein studies
★ Most unexplained adult cases → **kidney biopsy**; classic childhood minimal change often treated empirically
Anti-PLA2R supports primary membranous disease; assess secondary causes and age-based cancer screening
Diabetes with retinopathy, gradually rising albuminuria → likely diabetic nephropathy; atypical features → consider biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Salt restriction, **loop diuretic**, ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria; monitor perfusion and K
Eligible CKD → SGLT2 inhibitor; treat diabetes/infection or remove causative drug
Minimal change/primary FSGS → glucocorticoids; secondary FSGS → cause-directed/supportive treatment, not routine steroids
Membranous disease → risk-stratified observation versus rituximab or other immunosuppression
★ Confirmed thrombosis → anticoagulate; preventive anticoagulation individualized by albumin, pathology and bleeding risk

rows.label: Complications
items: DVT/PE, renal vein thrombosis, cellulitis/peritonitis, AKI, accelerated atherosclerosis
Progressive glomerular scarring can lead to kidney failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccinate, control BP/glycemia, avoid NSAIDs; monitor treatment toxicity and recurrent proteinuria

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nephritic syndrome: dysmorphic RBCs/casts, hypertension, inflammatory sediment
Cirrhosis: low albumin without nephrotic protein loss

table.title: Classic pathology
rows: Diffuse foot-process effacement; normal light microscopy

nephrotic-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching and risk-based treatment principles.

neural-tube-defects.name: Neural tube defects
neural-tube-defects.scope: Anencephaly, spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, Chiari II malformation, maternal serum AFP, amniotic acetylcholinesterase, lemon and banana signs, folic acid prevention
neural-tube-defects.core: Neural tube closure failure by approximately 4 weeks after conception produces cranial or spinal defects; prevention must begin before pregnancy recognition.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low folate, prior affected pregnancy, maternal diabetes/obesity, valproate/carbamazepine, early-pregnancy hyperthermia

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline lumbosacral sac, lower-limb weakness, absent reflexes, bladder dysfunction with neural involvement
★ **Lemon skull and banana cerebellum** on fetal ultrasound suggest open spina bifida/Chiari II
Occult lesions: hair tuft, atypical deep dimple, hemangioma; normal skin does not guarantee normal cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Failed neurulation leaves neural tissue unprotected; CSF leakage contributes to hindbrain herniation
Folate supports nucleotide synthesis during rapid embryonic cell division

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal serum **AFP at 15–22 weeks**; elevation → verify dating/number, detailed ultrasound
Open defects elevate AFP; closed occulta may not; cfDNA does not screen neural tube defects
★ Uncertain imaging → amniotic fluid **AFP and acetylcholinesterase**; target anatomy scan at 18–22 weeks
Postnatal spinal ultrasound in young infant or MRI for suspected occult dysraphism/tethered cord

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open spinal lesion: **prone positioning, sterile saline dressing**, avoid pressure/contamination; neonatal neurosurgery
Early closure; assess hydrocephalus, renal function and bladder emptying; intermittent catheterization when neurogenic
Selected prenatal myelomeningocele repair can improve motor outcomes/reduce shunting, with maternal and prematurity risks
Anencephaly → counseling, pregnancy options, and palliative neonatal care; no curative treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Hydrocephalus (Chiari II obstructs CSF), meningitis, orthopedic deformities, neurogenic bowel/bladder, recurrent UTI, kidney injury
Tethered cord may cause progressive weakness or continence changes during growth
Osteopenic insensate legs: new swelling → **X-ray** for occult fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Folic acid 400–800 µg/day** before conception through early pregnancy for average risk
Prior NTD pregnancy → **4 mg/day**, starting ≥1 month before conception through first 3 months
Optimize diabetes, review antiseizure drugs before pregnancy; avoid prolonged overheating

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sacrococcygeal teratoma: solid/cystic mass, not exposed neural placode
Abdominal wall defect: elevated AFP but bowel outside abdomen on ultrasound

table.title: Lesions
rows: Meninges/CSF herniate; cord remains within canal

neural-tube-defects.evidence: Folate checked 2026-10-30: [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/hcp/clinical-overview/), [USPSTF 2023](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/ClinicalSummaryFinal/folic-acid-for-the-prevention-of-neural-tube-defects-preventive-medication); remaining content established teaching.

obstructive-sleep-apnea.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
obstructive-sleep-apnea.scope: risk factors, clinical features (excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring), polysomnography, CPAP, cardiovascular complications
obstructive-sleep-apnea.core: Recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causes intermittent hypoxemia and arousals, often presenting as loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, aging, retrognathia and upper-airway crowding
Alcohol/sedatives worsen collapse; children often have adenotonsillar hypertrophy; risk rises after menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed apneas, gasping/choking, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia
Resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, secondary polycythemia or recurrent drowsy-driving episodes raise suspicion
Children may show hyperactivity, learning problems, enuresis or poor growth rather than sleepiness
Normal awake oxygen saturation does not exclude severe nocturnal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sleep-related reduction in pharyngeal tone collapses vulnerable airway despite persistent respiratory effort
Intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges drive hypertension; fragmentation impairs attention and vigilance
Sleep-related hypoventilation with nocturnal hypercapnia → morning headaches

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Polysomnography** confirms; screening tools such as STOP-BANG estimate risk, not diagnosis
Uncomplicated high-risk adults → home sleep apnea test acceptable; negative/inconclusive → in-laboratory study
★ AHI **≥5/hour with symptoms/comorbidity**, or ≥15 regardless of symptoms, establishes adult OSA
AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; pediatric thresholds differ
Cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, chronic opioids or neuromuscular weakness → laboratory polysomnography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CPAP** for symptomatic OSA and most moderate/severe disease; optimize mask fit/adherence
Weight loss, exercise, lateral sleep positioning; avoid bedtime alcohol and sedatives
★ CPAP-intolerant or selected mild/moderate disease → **mandibular advancement device**
Child adenotonsillar hypertrophy → adenotonsillectomy, even with pulmonary hypertension; selected adults → surgery, hypoglossal stimulation
Counsel sleepy patients to avoid driving until controlled; do not rely on stimulants before treating obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke risk, pulmonary hypertension in selected patients
Motor vehicle/work accidents, impaired cognition, mood disturbance
Awake postoperative hypercapnia → **CPAP/BiPAP**; reintubate only if obtunded or failing noninvasive support

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight, reassess after major weight change; continue PAP around surgery with monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central apnea: absent respiratory effort during pauses
Narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleep-onset REM features
OHS: persistent daytime hypercapnia

opioid-toxicity.name: Opioid toxicity
opioid-toxicity.scope: Opioid toxidrome, naloxone administration and titration, observation period, precipitated withdrawal
opioid-toxicity.core: Depressed consciousness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils after opioid exposure; ventilation takes priority over full awakening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fentanyl or heroin exposure, dose escalation, renal dysfunction, long-acting opioids
Alcohol/benzodiazepine co-ingestion; lost tolerance after detoxification, hospitalization, or incarceration

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Bradypnea or apnea** with hypoxemia; reduced bowel sounds, bradycardia, hypotension
Miosis may be absent with severe hypoxia or co-ingestion; needle marks are not required
Pulmonary edema, aspiration, hypothermia, prolonged immobilization may accompany overdose
Chronic use: daytime sleepiness, constipation, apathy, falling grades, miosis, slow breathing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mu-receptor activation suppresses medullary ventilatory response to CO2
Naloxone competitively reverses opioid effects but often wears off before the causative opioid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bedside glucose, pulse oximetry, capnography; do not await toxicology
Urine opiate immunoassay detects morphine/heroin/codeine; may miss fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone
ECG for methadone-associated QT prolongation; acetaminophen level with uncertain combination-product ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open airway, **bag-mask ventilation**, oxygen; intubate if ventilation cannot be maintained
★ **Naloxone** IV titrated to adequate breathing; intranasal/IM route if IV unavailable
Dependent but breathing: start low; apnea/no response: prompt larger/repeated doses, especially fentanyl analogs
Repeated recurrence → naloxone infusion; coma despite repeated doses → evaluate additional causes
Short-acting reversal: observe ≥4 hours after last naloxone; long-acting/recurrent sedation → prolonged monitoring/admission

rows.label: Complications
items: Anoxic brain injury, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome
Precipitated withdrawal: agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia; rare pulmonary edema after reversal

rows.label: Prevention
items: Take-home naloxone, overdose-response training, avoid sedative combinations; offer buprenorphine and addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pontine hemorrhage: focal neurologic findings, no meaningful naloxone response
Clonidine poisoning: marked bradycardia with similar pupils
Sedative overdose: usually normal pupils; incomplete naloxone response

parasitic-infections.name: Parasitic infections
parasitic-infections.scope: Strongyloidiasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis, pinworm (enterobiasis), cysticercosis, eosinophilia workup, antiparasitic therapy
parasitic-infections.core: Exposure, organ pattern, and immune status identify the parasite; eosinophilia favors tissue-invasive helminths rather than intestinal protozoa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Contaminated food/water, endemic travel, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, household crowding
Steroids/HTLV-1 predispose to Strongyloides hyperinfection; advanced HIV predisposes to persistent cryptosporidiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascariasis: transient cough/eosinophilic infiltrates during larval migration; later intestinal or biliary obstruction
Pinworm: nocturnal perianal/vulvar itch, dysuria with normal UA; household clustering
Cysticercosis: seizures or hydrocephalus; ingestion of **T. solium eggs**, not pork cysts
Cutaneous larva migrans: soil contact; pruritic **serpiginous tracks**; animal hookworm larvae → albendazole or ivermectin

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Giardia blunts microvilli → **fat/carbohydrate malabsorption**; invasive protozoa can affect liver, urinary tract, or CNS
Strongyloides autoinfection permits lifelong persistence and dissemination after immunosuppression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unexplained **eosinophilia** → travel/drug history, serial stool O&P, targeted Strongyloides serology
★ Steroids + eosinophilia or infiltrates → **Strongyloides hyperinfection**: **duodenal aspirate** larvae; stool O&P often misses
Diarrhea → stool antigen/PCR for protozoa; single routine O&P can miss infection
★ Pinworm → **morning tape test** before washing; stool testing insensitive
Brain MRI/CT for cysticercosis; eye examination before antiparasitics; assess lesion viability and location

rows.label: Tx
items: Rehydrate; ascariasis → albendazole; bowel obstruction → surgical evaluation before deworming
Pinworm → albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel; repeat after **2 weeks**, treat household simultaneously
★ Viable parenchymal cysticercosis → albendazole ± praziquantel with corticosteroids; seizures → levetiracetam
Calcified brain lesions → no antiparasitic; hydrocephalus → neurosurgical control before cysticidal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Strongyloides hyperinfection → gram-negative sepsis, respiratory failure; eosinophilia may disappear
Amebic liver abscess; schistosomiasis → portal hypertension or bladder squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen/treat Strongyloides before **immunosuppression** after endemic exposure
Safe water, sanitation, handwashing, footwear; avoid endemic freshwater and untreated swimming water
Neurocysticercosis household contacts → **stool O&P** to find egg-shedding T. solium tapeworm carrier

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea after infection excluded
Drug hypersensitivity: eosinophilia linked to new medication, rash or organ injury

table.title: Exposure → diagnosis and treatment
rows: Camping; greasy stool, bloating; stool antigen
Dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers; stool PCR; abscess → serology
Soil; larva currens, larvae in stool
Ivermectin; hyperinfection requires prolonged daily treatment
Freshwater; hematuria (haematobium), portal fibrosis (mansoni/japonicum); eggs, serology
Confirmed E. histolytica without invasive disease

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion, limited internal rotation/abduction; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**: gait, rotation, fever; limited rotation → **hip x-ray**, not knee MRI
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

table.title: Imaging and definitive branch
rows: Sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation; decreased bone-scan uptake

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

peripheral-neuropathy.name: Peripheral neuropathy
peripheral-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, chemotherapy-induced (cisplatin, paclitaxel), HIV-associated neuropathy, alcohol-related, neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy (TCAs, gabapentinoids, SNRIs)
peripheral-neuropathy.core: Length-dependent injury produces symmetric distal sensory symptoms beginning in the feet and progressing proximally before the hands become involved.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, alcohol use, CKD, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, HIV
Cisplatin/paclitaxel exposure; older neurotoxic ART such as stavudine; malnutrition

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning pain, allodynia or numbness; reduced vibration, ankle reflexes and distal sensation
★ **Asymmetry, rapid progression, motor predominance or marked autonomic findings** → urgent expanded evaluation
Small-fiber neuropathy: pain/temperature loss with initially preserved strength and nerve conduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Axonal dying-back affects longest fibers first; demyelinating neuropathy produces disproportionate conduction slowing

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose/A1c, B12 with methylmalonic acid if borderline, SPEP with immunofixation**
CBC, metabolic panel, TSH; HIV testing according to exposure and clinical context
EMG/nerve conduction for atypical features, unclear diagnosis, or suspected demyelination
Normal studies do not exclude small-fiber disease; skin biopsy can confirm selected cases

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat cause: glycemic control, B12, alcohol cessation/nutrition, optimize ART; review neurotoxic drugs
★ Pain → **duloxetine, gabapentin/pregabalin, or TCA**; choose by comorbidity and adverse effects
Gabapentinoids: sedation/edema, renal dose adjustment; TCAs: anticholinergic effects, cardiac risk in older adults
★ Painful chemotherapy neuropathy → **duloxetine**; discuss dose reduction/substitution with oncology
Topical lidocaine/capsaicin for localized symptoms; avoid chronic opioids

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, painless ulcers, infection, Charcot arthropathy; orthostatic hypotension with autonomic involvement
Pain treatment reduces symptoms without restoring lost sensation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Daily foot inspection, protective footwear, monofilament assessment, fall prevention
Treat nutritional deficiencies; monitor symptoms during neurotoxic chemotherapy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Radiculopathy: dermatomal, often asymmetric pain and weakness
Myelopathy: hyperreflexia, sensory level, bowel/bladder dysfunction
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses rather than sensory stocking loss
Charcot-Marie-Tooth: adolescent **pes cavus, hammer toes**, distal wasting, slowed conduction, family history

pertussis.name: Pertussis
pertussis.scope: Bordetella pertussis, catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, posttussive emesis, inspiratory whoop, macrolide therapy, postexposure prophylaxis, Tdap vaccination
pertussis.core: Prolonged paroxysmal cough with posttussive emesis; infants may present with apnea and cyanosis without a whoop.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unvaccinated/undervaccinated children, waning immunity in adolescents/adults, infected household contacts
Young infants have greatest risk of severe disease; vaccinated individuals can still transmit infection

rows.label: Clues
items: Catarrhal stage: rhinorrhea, mild cough, little or no fever; greatest early infectiousness
Inspiratory whoop often absent in adolescents/adults; convalescence can last weeks with recurrent cough
★ Infant **marked lymphocytosis**, poor feeding, or respiratory compromise; minimal fever despite serious illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: B. pertussis adheres to respiratory cilia; toxin-mediated injury impairs mucus clearance
Pertussis toxin inhibits Gi signaling; impaired lymphocyte extravasation causes circulating lymphocytosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Nasopharyngeal PCR** during first 3–4 weeks of cough; posterior nasopharynx, not throat swab
Culture most useful in first 2 weeks; late illness → validated serology when available
Treat suspected high-risk cases before results; chest imaging for respiratory compromise or suspected pneumonia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Azithromycin** preferred; TMP-SMX alternative at age ≥2 months when macrolides unsuitable
Best symptom benefit early; later treatment mainly reduces transmission within infectious window
Treat age ≥1 year within 3 weeks of cough; infants/pregnancy up to 6 weeks
Hospitalize young infants or apnea/hypoxemia; oxygen, suction, hydration and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Infant macrolides carry pyloric stenosis risk, but benefit outweighs risk; monitor vomiting

rows.label: Complications
items: Pneumonia, seizures/encephalopathy, infant pulmonary hypertension and death
Adults: rib fractures, syncope, stress incontinence from forceful coughing

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Droplet isolation until **5 days of effective antibiotics**, or 21 days from cough onset untreated
Household contacts → azithromycin prophylaxis within 21 days of index cough; also target high-risk exposures
DTaP childhood series; Tdap adolescent booster and once for adults without prior Tdap
★ **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 weeks**, preferably early in that interval

rows.label: Mimics
